opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the reason I find this one compelling is that it doesn't require anyone to do anything dramatic or obviously evil. A lot of people's mental model of how humans stay okay after transformative AI is something like: "Well, even if our labor isn't worth anything anymore, we'll own stuff. We'll own land, shares, houses, and we can live off that." And I think that's a much more fragile position than it sounds.

Think about what a property or land tax actually is. It's a recurring charge just for holding onto something. Right now that's fine for most people because they have income from work to pay it. But in a world where human labor is basically uncompetitive, a lot of people become asset-rich and income-poor, like a retiree who owns a house in a neighborhood that's suddenly gentrifying. Their property tax goes up, they don't have the cash flow, and they have to sell. Nobody stole the house. They were just slowly squeezed out by perfectly ordinary, legal mechanisms.

Now scale that up. If AI-driven growth makes land and physical resources enormously valuable, because you want them for data centers, energy, manufacturing, whatever, then land values could rise faster than whatever passive income humans are getting. And governments will have very strong incentives to tax those assets, because they need revenue, and also because economists already tend to like land taxes as efficient. There's a respectable argument that idle land held by people who aren't using it productively should be taxed so it goes to its highest-value use. And in an AI economy, the highest-value use is almost never going to be "a human lives there and grows tomatoes."

The other piece is political. Today, if a government did something that pushed huge numbers of people off their land, there'd be pushback, and that pushback matters because the state depends on those people: for tax revenue, for labor, for soldiers, for legitimacy. As that dependence weakens, because the state's revenue increasingly comes from AI-run firms, the people being squeezed have less leverage. So it's not that anyone decides to expropriate humans. It's that the ordinary pressures that used to protect them quietly stop working.

So property taxes are just a nice, concrete example of the general pattern I worry about. You don't need a coup or a rogue AI. You just need a bunch of individually reasonable policies in an economy where humans have stopped being necessary, and the default outcome is that our share of resources erodes over time. Owning stuff only protects you as long as the system keeps respecting and enforcing that ownership on terms you can actually afford.

r001.rationale: The response connects a retiree being priced out by rising property taxes in a gentrifying neighborhood to AI-era policies that tax land toward higher-value, more productive uses.

r002.rationale: The response discusses selling assets and losing leverage, but does not suggest that tax pressure could lead humans to upload themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the usual optimistic story goes something like: even if AIs end up doing almost all the economically valuable work, humans still own things. We own land, we own capital, we own shares in the companies that own the AIs. And as long as property rights are respected, we just sit back and collect rents. The economy grows enormously, our assets appreciate, everyone's fine.

And I think that story has a hole in it, which is that property rights aren't free. Owning something isn't a one-time event — it's an ongoing relationship with a state that chooses to enforce your claim, and the state charges you for that in the form of taxes. Right now, property taxes and land taxes are usually a small fraction of the value of the asset, maybe one or two percent a year. That's fine when your income from the asset, or from your labour, comfortably covers the bill.

But imagine a world where humans basically have no labour income, because AIs do everything better and cheaper. And imagine the state has an enormous demand for revenue — maybe to fund its own AI capabilities, maybe for defence, maybe just because the actors who are actually productive, which are AIs or AI-run firms, are the ones with political influence. Then the natural place to raise revenue is from assets that are just sitting there in the hands of people who aren't producing anything. And a tax of a few percent a year on wealth, sustained over decades, is a very effective way to transfer that wealth to whoever the state actually answers to. Nobody has to confiscate anything. There's no dramatic moment where humans lose their property. You just can't pay the bill, so you sell a little bit each year, and the entities that can pay — because they're earning — are the ones buying.

What I find worrying about this is it doesn't require anyone to be malicious or for AIs to be misaligned. It's just the ordinary machinery of a tax system responding to where the money is and who's politically relevant. We've seen versions of this historically: groups that lost economic relevance tended to lose their assets gradually, through perfectly legal mechanisms, rather than being expropriated outright. So when people say "humans will be fine because we own the capital," my question is: own it according to whom, and at what annual cost? Because that cost is set by a political process, and in the scenario we're talking about, humans are no longer the ones with leverage in that process.

r001.rationale: The response describes tax-driven asset transfers from people without income to productive AI-run entities, but it does not connect this to today’s property or land taxes displacing older homeowners in favor of occupants viewed as more productive.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that tax-driven wealth loss could pressure humans to upload themselves.

astra-6.text:
Well, even if humans retain ownership of land, that doesn’t necessarily mean they can afford to keep it. You have to pay property taxes, and those can go up as the assessed value of the property goes up.

Imagine an AI economy where there’s an enormous amount of productive activity, and land becomes much more valuable. You might own a house somewhere that AIs would like to build a factory or a data centre. If your tax bill reflects what they’re willing to pay for that land, but your income hasn’t kept up—perhaps because your labour is no longer worth much—you could be forced to sell.

Now, you do get money from selling. So this isn’t, by itself, a story where everyone immediately loses everything. And if you can rent out the land, the higher rents could cover the tax. But it illustrates why having property rights isn’t quite the same as having a guaranteed, permanent claim on resources. There are ongoing obligations attached to ownership, and those obligations are set by political institutions.

The concern is that humans could gradually get priced out through perfectly ordinary economic and legal processes. You don’t need an AI to come along and explicitly confiscate your house.

r001.rationale: The response says rising assessments could force owners to sell to AIs seeking valuable land, but it does not connect this to today’s practice of displacing older homeowners in favor of more productive occupants.

r002.rationale: It describes possible forced sales and loss of a permanent claim to resources, but does not suggest that this could pressure humans to upload themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that owning something doesn’t necessarily mean you can afford to keep it. Suppose you own your house, and you’re imagining that even if AI makes your labour worthless, at least you’ll still have somewhere to live. You still have to pay property taxes. And if the value of that land goes up enormously because AI systems can put it to much more productive use, the tax bill could become more than you can afford.

You could sell it, of course, and initially that might leave you quite wealthy. But the broader point is that property rights exist within a system of ongoing obligations. They’re not a guarantee that humans can retain some fixed share of the physical world indefinitely, especially if we no longer have much earning power.

That’s not to say this outcome is inevitable. We could change the tax rules or redistribute the proceeds. But you need some mechanism like that; simply saying “humans will still own the land” doesn’t settle the question.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains how AI-driven increases in land value could make property taxes unaffordable, but does not connect this to current tax-driven displacement of older homeowners in favor of more productive occupants.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses selling property and changing tax or redistribution rules, but does not suggest that tax-driven wealth loss could pressure humans to upload themselves.
